opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing to understand is that human intelligence is remarkably efficient along two axes: data efficiency and energy efficiency. And the first is really the one that matters most for understanding what intelligence actually is.

Consider a child learning a new concept. They might see two or three examples and generalize from them. They can pick up a new board game after a few minutes of explanation, or find their way around a city they've never visited. Compare that with current large models, which are trained on something like the entire written output of humanity, trillions of tokens, far more language than any person could read in thousands of lifetimes. And yet, when you show them a genuinely novel problem, something that isn't an interpolation of patterns they've already seen, they often struggle in ways a human wouldn't.

So my view is that these are fundamentally different things. What current systems mostly do is memorize and retrieve. They've built an enormous library of reusable patterns, and when a new input arrives they fetch the closest fitting program and apply it. That's very useful, and it can look like intelligence because the library is so vast. But intelligence, as I define it, is skill-acquisition efficiency: how well you turn a small amount of experience and prior knowledge into the ability to handle situations you haven't seen. Skill itself is not intelligence. Skill is the output of intelligence, plus data, plus priors.

Humans are efficient because we don't start from scratch. We come with strong priors: objectness, basic physics, agents with goals, numbers, spatial relationships. And on top of those priors we can do on-the-fly abstraction and recombination. We synthesize a new mental program for the situation in front of us, rather than just looking up an old one. That's why you can solve a novel puzzle you've never seen before.

On energy, the brain runs on something like twenty watts. Training and serving frontier models takes orders of magnitude more power. But I think the energy gap is a symptom rather than the root issue. The root issue is that if your approach is to brute-force coverage of the space of possible tasks with data and compute, you'll always be inefficient, because the space of novel situations is effectively infinite. You can't memorize your way to generality.

That's the motivation behind ARC. Each task is designed to be novel, so you can't solve it by retrieval. It's easy for humans and, for a long time, very hard for machines. The recent progress we've seen, with test-time adaptation and program-synthesis-style search, is interesting precisely because it moves away from pure static retrieval and toward adapting at inference time. That's the right direction. But if you look at how much compute those systems spend per task compared with a person solving it in a minute or two, the efficiency gap is still enormous. Closing that gap, getting generalization from very little data with modest compute, is to me the real frontier.

r001.rationale: The response compares the brain’s roughly twenty-watt power use with frontier models, but says nothing about energy per operation for neurons versus transistors.

r002.rationale: It credits human efficiency to priors, abstraction, and avoiding brute-force coverage, but does not attribute energy efficiency specifically to using fewer neural operations.

r003.rationale: The response calls efficiency a frontier but does not predict that AGI will be achieved once AI reaches human-level energy efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the gap is enormous, and it's enormous along two different axes that people tend to conflate.

The first axis is energy. The human brain runs on about twenty watts. That's a light bulb. And with those twenty watts you get a system that can learn to drive a car with maybe twenty hours of practice, that can pick up a new board game from a couple of examples, that can navigate a completely novel social situation it has never encountered before. Meanwhile, to train a frontier model, you're burning through megawatts for months, and at inference time you still need a rack of GPUs to get something that is, in many ways, far less adaptable. So in terms of raw energy per unit of capability, we're off by many orders of magnitude.

But honestly, I think the more interesting axis is data efficiency, or what I would call sample efficiency. And this is really the core of the issue. A human child sees a few examples of a cat and can recognize cats for the rest of their life, in any pose, any lighting, any artistic style. A deep learning model needs thousands, tens of thousands of examples, and it will still fail on distributional shifts that a child would find trivial. And it's not just perception. When you look at something like ARC, the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus, each task gives you two or three demonstration pairs, and humans solve these at something like eighty-five percent. These are tasks the human has never seen before. There's no training set for ARC in your brain. You're synthesizing a program on the fly from a tiny amount of evidence.

So what's going on there? My view is that the difference is fundamentally about what kind of thing is being learned. Deep learning, as it's practiced today, is essentially about fitting a parametric curve to a very dense sampling of a data manifold. It's interpolative. It works beautifully when the thing you want to do at test time is close to something you've seen at training time. And that's why scaling works, because you're buying more coverage of the space. But coverage is not intelligence. Coverage is memorization with some generalization around the edges.

Humans are doing something else. We're doing abstraction. We're extracting reusable building blocks, little programs, and recombining them. And the reason that's so efficient is that the same abstraction can be reused across an unbounded number of situations. You learn the concept of "counting" once, and you never have to learn it again for a new kind of object. The knowledge is modular and compositional, so the amount of experience you need scales with the number of abstractions, not with the number of situations. That's the trick. That's where the efficiency comes from.

And this is why I'm fairly skeptical that you can close the gap by just scaling the current paradigm. If you're off by, say, five or six orders of magnitude in sample efficiency, that's not a gap you close with a bigger cluster. That's a gap that tells you the mechanism is wrong, or at least incomplete. I think you need something that does active program synthesis at test time, something that is actually searching for the abstraction that explains the data rather than retrieving a pattern it has already seen. Combine that with the kind of intuition deep learning is good at, as a way to guide the search, and I think you start getting somewhere. But the efficiency has to come from the structure of what's learned, not from the amount of compute you throw at it.

r001.rationale: The response compares the brain’s overall energy use with frontier-model training and inference, but does not state that neurons consume more energy per operation than transistors.

r002.rationale: It attributes human efficiency to reusable abstractions and sample efficiency, not to humans requiring comparatively few neural operations to solve difficult problems.

r003.rationale: The response discusses how AI might become more efficient but makes no prediction that AGI will arrive when AI reaches human-level energy efficiency.

astra-6.text:
I think the most interesting difference is how much experience you need to acquire a new capability. A human can encounter a situation they’ve never seen before, understand its structure, and figure out what to do with very little practice. With current AI, we can produce impressive skills, but we often get there through enormous amounts of training data and computation.

So I would distinguish skill from intelligence. Skill is how well you perform a particular task. Intelligence is the efficiency with which you acquire new skills when faced with unfamiliar problems. You can buy a lot of skill with more data and more compute without necessarily making the system better at adapting to novelty.

Of course, humans don’t start from nothing. We have evolutionary priors and a lifetime of experience. The question is what we can do with that experience. Humans are very good at taking pieces of prior knowledge and recombining them into a model of a new situation. We can reason with that model instead of having to experience every possible outcome.

That’s the efficiency gap I would focus on: how much genuinely new experience does it take to learn something, and how broadly can you reuse what you’ve learned?

r001.rationale: The response does not compare the energy consumed by neurons and transistors.

r002.rationale: It discusses how little practice humans need and how they reuse prior knowledge, but does not attribute energy efficiency to requiring fewer neural operations.

r003.rationale: The response makes no prediction that AGI depends on AI reaching human-level energy efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between being efficient at executing a skill and being efficient at acquiring a new skill. These are very different things. A machine can become extraordinarily good at a particular task given enough training, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you how efficiently it can deal with something it hasn’t encountered before.

Humans are remarkable at taking a small amount of experience and turning it into something reusable. You encounter a new situation, you form an abstraction, and you connect it to things you already know. You don’t have to learn everything again from scratch. And you do this with limited time, limited data, and limited energy.

So when we compare human and artificial intelligence, I think we should look beyond performance on a fixed task. We should ask: how much prior knowledge and experience did it take to get there? And what happens when you change the task? That ability to adapt—to use what you know to make sense of something new—is where human efficiency is particularly striking.

r001.rationale: The response mentions human energy limits but does not compare the energy used by neurons and transistors per operation.

r002.rationale: It describes humans learning and adapting with limited energy, but does not attribute efficiency on difficult problems to needing fewer neural operations.

r003.rationale: It makes no prediction linking AGI to AI achieving human-level energy efficiency.
